newsitem.title: USA: Just how big will New York City's tax revenues be?.
newsitem.headline: Just how big will New York City's tax revenues be?.

text.p: New York City's battle over a new budget Friday headed toward a showdown over how much extra money will be available, though the Giuliani Administration and the City Council also sparred over some planned cuts.

Budget Director Joseph Lhota, testifying before the Council's Finance committee, said: "In negotiations with the council, I told them we believe there is additional revenue this year." But he added that final numbers were not ready and offered no specifics.

Mayor Rudolph Giuliani already has predicted an $856 million surplus for fiscal 1997, which ends on June 30. The money will be rolled into the next fiscal year. New York City is expected to approve a new budget for fiscal 1998 as soon as late next week or around the June 10 target date.

A city source, who declined to be named, predicted that New York State Deputy Comptroller Rosemary Scanlon would forecast that the city would collect as much as $500 million more in fiscal 1997 and 1998, when she unveils her assessment of the mayor's budget plan next week. A spokeswoman for Scanlon was not immediately available to comment.

Council sources would not confirm any tax revenue estimates, but noted their forecast was significantly higher than both the mayor's and one from city Comptroller Alan Hevesi, who sees another $202 million in fiscal 1998.
One city source said New York City should have around $500 million more than Giuliani has estimated, once various risks have been taken into account.
"We probably do have a difference of opinion as to what the surplus will be this year that could be rolled over," said Herbert Berman, who chairs the Council's finance committee.
The Council wants to use the funds for a Rainy Day Fund, targeted tax cuts and boosting spending for youth services and cultural institutions.

Views that the Republican mayor's revenue estimates were too low were based on a number of factors. For example, city sources said a forecast that personal income tax collections would only rise 0.4 percent were far too low. And so was an estimate that Wall Street's profits would fall to $4.7 billion from $11.3 billion in the 1996 calender year, they said.

But Lhota refused to give an inch when questioned by Sheldon Leffler, who chairs the Public Safety Committee, saying the profits expected for Wall Street--a lynchpin industry for the city's economy--were a 10-year average.
Lhota noted that several years ago, this sector's profits plunged to $1.1 billion because banks and brokerage houses lost about $5.5 billion in about two weeks late in the year.

Later, Leffler, who said that the budget director should raise his estimates for the personal income and corporate taxes because Wall Street's earnings likely would surpass the mayor's estimates, argued: "But it's not sufficient to say you could lose it."

The city budget director reminded him the city charter gives the mayor the sole responsibility for determining revenues. Rating agencies have praised the mayor's budget plan for using conservative estimates.

Lhota was optimistic Albany will let the city eliminate its sales taxes for clothing that costs less than $500, saying the Republican Senate's leaders did not necessarily agree with fellow party members from nearby suburbs, who felt the city's stores would gain too big an edge.

Giuliani, pointing to the success of a one-week moratorium in January that was matched by the state and most localities, wants to eliminate the city levy for a two-week period just before the autumn school year, and end it in December.

While Lhota said his staff was working with the city comptroller to find more revenues and asset sales to make up for the $1 billion that the city hoped to get by selling its water system, other sources have not yet been identified. Hevesi objected to the proposed water sale, and the Guiliani Administration, who took the battle to court, lost the fight.

Though New York City's budget director saw a risk that overtime spending might have to be increased when a new youth detention center is opened early next year, he fought hard against views that there was extra money to spread around.
"We don't think you do a budget from year to year. We now focus on what we could do to deal with outyear gaps," he said.

The city's 1999 fiscal budget gap is estimated at nearly $2.0, and Leffler, pointing to this and wider outyear gaps, criticized the mayor giving voters a "sense of financial well-being" by focusing on the near-term surplus.
((--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650))
